With the M6 Mac mini and its more advanced M5 Pro counterpart now officially on sale, Apple has quietly removed one of the machine's most appealing selling points. Although both new Mac minis look identical to the previous generation on the outside, Apple has eliminated a hidden feature found on the last Mac mini — one that made it an exceptionally high-value model.

When the M4 Mac mini first launched, its value proposition was off the charts. Beyond Apple's own M4 SoC, the machine came standard with 16GB of unified memory, three Thunderbolt 4 ports, two front-facing USB 3 ports, HDMI, and Ethernet. Priced at US$599 (or just US$499 with the student discount), the M4 Mac mini was not only the most versatile Mac in Apple's entire lineup but also delivered the best overall performance.

Video: Apple Killed the Best Hidden Feature of the Mac mini :(

However, Apple's smallest Mac had another ace up its sleeve that made it an even better deal: a built-in, user-upgradable storage slot. Users only needed to pry off the back panel and remove a few screws to access a removable NAND module, which could easily be swapped out for a third-party SSD supporting up to 2TB.

This design came with many benefits. Not only could users upgrade their SSD or easily deal with drive failures, but they could also save a considerable amount of money — no need to opt for Apple's custom upgrade options; just buy a much cheaper third-party SSD and you're set.

Back then, Apple priced the 2TB upgrade at US$800, so ticking that option alone turned this "budget" computer into a US$1,400 machine. By purchasing the base model and then upgrading with a third-party SSD, users could save nearly US$500.

As someone who enjoys building PCs, I was naturally thrilled, and even produced a comprehensive step-by-step video tutorial showing how to upgrade the factory SSD with a third-party drive. The video was extremely well-received, racking up 500,000 views.

Video: How to Upgrade the SSD on M4 Mac mini

Those good times didn't last.

With this generation of Mac mini, Apple has soldered the SSD directly onto the logic board, completely eliminating the possibility of post-purchase upgrades using third-party NAND modules.

The Mac mini has gone from being the undisputed best-value Mac to a product that is noticeably much more expensive — not only has the base model jumped from US$600 to US$900, but the 2TB upgrade has also increased from US$800 to US$1,000.

At current pricing, if you want an M6 Mac mini with 2TB of SSD, you'll inevitably have to pay Apple US$1,900. Compared to the previous M4 Mac mini, which at the time could be upgraded to 2TB for around US$920 in total (including a roughly US$320 post-purchase upgrade), this is a full US$1,000 more expensive. Of course, prices fluctuate over time and can't be compared directly (you all know how Apple operates), but we're looking at a difference of a full US$1,000 here. Beyond Apple's steep price hikes, the bigger reason is that they've outright taken away users' right to upgrade the machine themselves.

I can roughly guess why Apple raised the base Mac mini's price by US$300, and the sharp increase in SSD prices is something I can also understand. Driven by factors such as AI, the costs of components, SSDs, and memory have all risen substantially. But none of this explains why Apple chose to solder the SSD to the logic board rather than retain the previous user-replaceable design.

Why would Apple decide to go back down the path of soldering the SSD in place? We can speculate, but we'll never know the real answer. What is certain is that the prices of these machines have soared — saying "soared" might even be an understatement. Comparing an M4 Mac mini from back in the day with a post-purchase 2TB upgrade to today's M6 Mac mini with a 2TB custom upgrade, the price has risen by approximately 106%.

9to5Mac Opinion

Finding a reasonably priced base-model M4 Mac mini on the second-hand market isn't easy these days, but if you do manage to track one down, it remains a truly outstanding machine in terms of performance, features, and upgradable SSD.

The only silver lining is that all Mac mini models come with Thunderbolt connectivity, allowing users to easily add high-speed external storage via USB or Thunderbolt SSDs. Personally, I'm particularly fond of the Samsung T9, which is a relatively affordable storage expansion solution.

Why do you think Apple abandoned the user-replaceable SSD design on the Mac mini? Do you have any unique insights? Feel free to share your views in the comments section.
